back: A tissue made of muscle cells whose cytoplasm is packed with contractile filaments (actin and myosin).

front: Classify the three muscle types histologically and physiologically.
back: Histologically: striated (skeletal, cardiac) vs non-striated (smooth). Physiologically: voluntary (skeletal) vs involuntary (cardiac, smooth). Cardiac is striated but involuntary.
The cytoplasm of a muscle cell.
The (smooth) endoplasmic reticulum of a muscle cell; it stores and releases Ca²⁺.
A mitochondrion of a muscle cell.
The cell membrane (plasmalemma) of a muscle cell.
Myofiber = the whole muscle cell (muscle fiber). Myofibril = a long subunit inside the cell, made of a chain of sarcomeres.

front: How do longitudinal and transverse sections of muscle look? (membujur vs melintang)
back: Longitudinal (membujur): long parallel strips. Transverse (melintang): round or polygonal islands. In the atlas figure, OL = transverse, IC = longitudinal.
Fusiform (spindle) cells, no cross-striations, one elongated nucleus in the center of the cell.
Walls of blood vessels, GI tract, respiratory tract, uterus, urinary bladder and other internal organs (also arrector pili, iris). Also called visceral muscle.
Autonomic nervous system; the myoneural junction is called a synapse. Contraction is slow and involuntary.

front: Why do smooth muscle cross-sections show profiles of different sizes, only some with nuclei?
back: The cells are spindle-shaped: cuts through the thick middle are large and include the central nucleus; cuts through the tapered ends are small and have none.
Smooth muscle: spindle cells, no striations, central elongated nuclei.

front: Skeletal muscle: other names and control.
back: Striated or cross-striated muscle (otot lurik, otot rangka). Voluntary; contraction triggered by acetylcholine at the motor end plate (neuromuscular junction).
Long cylindrical fibers, multinucleated; oval nuclei located peripherally, just beneath the clearly visible sarcolemma.

front: Epimysium, perimysium, endomysium: what does each wrap, and what is it made of?
back: Epimysium: the whole muscle (dense irregular CT). Perimysium: a fascicle (dense irregular CT). Endomysium: each fiber (fine reticular fibers).
The island-like pattern of myofibril bundles seen inside a skeletal muscle fiber cut in cross-section.

front: Identify this and name the pattern inside each fiber.
back: Skeletal muscle in transverse section; the stippled islands inside each fiber are Cohnheim's areas.
A band: dark, anisotropic, contains myosin (thick filaments). I band: light, isotropic, contains actin only (thin filaments).

front: Z line, M line and H zone: where is each?
back: Z line: dark line in the center of the I band. M line: dark line in the center of the A band. H zone: lighter region in the center of the A band.
The segment from one Z line to the next: the smallest contractile unit of striated muscle.

front: Name the dark and light bands.
back: Dark = A band (anisotropic); light = I band (isotropic).
Limited: fibers cannot divide, but satellite cells can repair small injuries. Larger losses heal with scar.
Parallel striated fibers that branch and anastomose; intercalated discs (irregular dark transverse lines); one (sometimes two) large, oval, central nucleus.
Irregular dark transverse lines marking junctions between cardiac muscle cells; they contain desmosomes, fasciae adherentes and gap junctions.

front: Identify this tissue and the structure labeled I.
back: Cardiac muscle; I = intercalated disc (N = nucleus).

front: What is the branching and rejoining of cardiac fibers called?
back: Anastomosis (intercellular anastomosis; Indonesian: anastomose serabut otot).
Essentially none: after an infarct, dead muscle is replaced by fibrous scar.

front: Smooth vs cardiac vs skeletal: nucleus position.
back: Smooth: one, central. Cardiac: one or two, central. Skeletal: many, peripheral (beneath the sarcolemma).

front: Smooth vs cardiac vs skeletal: location.
back: Smooth: walls of the gut and hollow organs. Cardiac: heart. Skeletal: limbs (extremities) and trunk.

front: Three layers of the skin and their origin.
back: Epidermis (ectoderm), dermis (mesoderm), and beneath them the hypodermis (subcutis).

front: What type of epithelium is the epidermis, and how is it nourished?
back: Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium; it has no vessels and is nourished by diffusion from the dermis.

front: Strata of thin skin, deep to superficial.
back: Stratum basale, spinosum, granulosum, corneum (no lucidum).

front: Strata of thick skin, deep to superficial.
back: Stratum basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum, corneum.

A single layer of cuboidal or columnar basophilic cells, attached to the basal lamina by hemidesmosomes and to each other by desmosomes; high mitotic activity, with progenitor cells for all epidermal cells.
Several layers of polygonal cells joined by desmosomes, which look like spines; tonofibrils run into them. Langerhans cells live here. With the basale it forms the stratum Malpighii.

front: Which layer is boxed, and what do the yellow arrows mark?
back: Stratum spinosum; the yellow arrows mark tonofibrils.
3–5 layers of flattened cells with dark keratohyalin granules; lamellar granules secrete lipid that waterproofs the skin. Cells die above this layer.
Several layers of flattened, pale, anucleate cells containing eleidin droplets. Found only in thick skin.
15–20 layers of flattened, dead, anucleate cells filled with refractile keratin; the surface is shed (desquamation).
Thick skin (palms, soles): very thick corneum, stratum lucidum, no hair or sebaceous glands. Thin skin (elsewhere): thin corneum, no lucidum, hair follicles and sebaceous glands.

front: Thick or thin skin? Which layer proves it?
back: Thick skin: the stratum lucidum (plus a very thick corneum).
Round cell body with long processes, between the cells of the stratum basale; produces eumelanin and passes it to keratinocytes.

front: Does dark skin have more melanocytes?
back: No: the number is similar; dark skin makes and transfers more melanin.

front: Identify the cells at the blue arrows.
back: Melanocytes: pale cells among the basal keratinocytes.
Looks like a melanocyte but makes no melanin; mainly in the stratum spinosum; macrophage-like immune (antigen-presenting) cell.
Resembles a keratinocyte with small dense granules; in the basal layer, especially thick skin; with its nerve ending it forms the Merkel corpuscle, a mechanoreceptor.
Mostly immature T lymphocytes (round cells, dense nuclei), whose maturation keratinocytes support. With Langerhans cells and keratinocytes they form SALT, skin-associated lymphoid tissue.

front: Stratum papillare of the dermis: tissue and contents.
back: Thin, loose connective tissue: fibroblasts, macrophages, mast cells; dermal papillae interlocking with epidermal ridges; capillaries that feed the epidermis; anchoring fibrils (type VII collagen); Meissner's corpuscles.

front: Stratum reticulare of the dermis: tissue and fibers.
back: Thick, dense irregular connective tissue: mainly type I collagen and elastic fibers.
Loose connective tissue with abundant adipocytes, extensive blood supply, and Pacinian corpuscles (pressure receptors). Also called subcutis.
Unencapsulated; a free nerve ending attached to a Merkel cell in the basal epidermis; light touch / tactile sensation.
Oval, onion-like; capsule of concentric lamellae (collagen and flattened endothelium-like cells); deep dermis and subcutis; crude touch, sustained pressure and vibration.

front: Identify the structures at the arrows, and what they sense.
back: Vater-Pacini corpuscles: pressure and vibration.
Cylindrical; branched encapsulated endings in a thin capsule of transversely arranged flattened cells; in the dermal papillae; light touch.
Cylindrical, smaller than Meissner; spray-like branching inside a thin capsule; in the dermis; pressure.
Round; branched encapsulated endings in a thick capsule; in the dermis; pressure (practicum; older texts: cold).
Hair shaft (above the skin), hair root (within the follicle) and hair bulb (expanded base with dermal papilla, blood vessels, dividing epithelial cells and melanocytes).

front: Layers of the hair from the inside out.
back: Medulla, cortex, cuticle.

front: The two parts of the follicle sheath, and what separates them.
back: Outer dermal (connective tissue) root sheath, where the arrector pili attaches, and inner epidermal (epithelial) root sheath, separated by the glassy membrane.
A hair follicle in transverse section.
A small bundle of smooth muscle from the dermal root sheath to the papillary dermis; contraction raises the hair (goosebumps) and helps express sebum.
Simple branched acinar; holocrine (the whole cell becomes sebum); opens into the hair follicle (pilosebaceous unit). Absent from palms and soles.

front: Identify this gland and its mode of secretion.
back: Sebaceous gland; holocrine secretion.

front: Eccrine sweat gland: shape, secretion, opening.
back: Simple coiled tubular; merocrine; secretory portion in the deep dermis (dark and clear cells plus myoepithelial cells); duct of 2-layered cuboidal epithelium opens onto the skin surface at a sweat pore.
Flat contractile cells between the secretory cells and the basal lamina of the secretory portion (not the duct); they squeeze secretion out.
Larger coiled tubular gland with a wide lumen; opens into a hair follicle; axilla, areola, anogenital region; active after puberty.

front: Eccrine vs apocrine vs sebaceous: where does each open?
back: Eccrine: skin surface. Apocrine: hair follicle. Sebaceous: hair follicle.
A keratin plate on the dorsal distal phalanx, resting on the nail bed; eponychium (cuticle) at the proximal end, hyponychium under the free distal edge; produced by the nail matrix under the root.
